newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa's "city of gold" tries to revive its heart.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa's "city of gold" tries to revive its heart.

text.p: South Africa's "city of gold", Johannesburg, set off on Thursday on a journey to restore faith in its future with the launch of a two billion rand ($440 million) project to revitalise the inner city.
About 4,000 people packed Library Gardens, scene of bloody political clashes ahead of the 1994 democracy elections, to cheer the initiative in a city that has been South Africa's economic powerhouse.

Johannesburg contributes about 25 percent to the entire South African gross domestic product, officials say, but years of neglect have turned its once fashionable downtown business district into a shadow of its former self.

Criminals have accompanied the poor, the homeless and the street hawkers who have moved in as largely white-run businesses, restaurants and shops move out to affluent suburbs -- or even to more relaxed and scenic Cape Town.
Since the discovery late last century of gold where Johannesburg now stands, people from as far afield as Zambia, Angola and Mozambique have continued to flock here in search of work and prosperity.

Both ideals have proven elusive to some, thus fuelling inner city blight, poverty and crime. Big-name banks and insurance houses have stayed in the city but many of their neighbours have moved out. At night it is largely deserted.
President Nelson Mandela's lieutenant, Deputy President Thabo Mbeki, told the gathering that Johannesburg, branded locally as the "crime capital of the world", wanted to reclaim its past splendour.
"Today the city of Johannesburg is beginning the process of its rebirth," he said.

"For a century it has stood at the heart of the process of the birth of our nation...because it attracted to itself all our people, regardless of language, culture, colour, gender and ethnic origins."

Government, business and local communities aim together to turn Johannesburg's inner city into a hub of economic and cultural activity, house its homeless, and provide a safer investment centre for the whole of southern Africa.

"Our objectives are not just a wish list. Johannesburg has to be a welcoming destination. A city to which people can come to invest, (and) rise from poverty," said Colin Matjila, leader of Johannesburg's Metro Council Executive Committee.
The renewal project involves the creation of a metropolitan police force by next year to aid the national police in urban crime prevention.
Some eight million rand has also been earmarked to build eight shelters to house the city's 7,000 homeless and 200 million rand to revamp Johannesburg central railway station.
A 600-bed hostel is also to be built to accommodate informal traders who have got used to braving the night on the pavement, to wake up and sell their wares the next morning.
Philemon Tenehi, 35, from the Soweto township some 15 km (10 miles) away, hoped the renewal project could help him find work.
"I feel proud today when I hear about this project. Many people thought Johannesburg had lost its value. I believe people would come back now and give us work. This is progress," he told Reuters.
